item.title: How an Uncertain Economy Affects Gen Z’s Budgeting
item.description:
Behavioral Economics

How an Uncertain Economy Affects Gen Z’s Budgeting

Budgeting isn’t just about money. It’s about psychology.

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Gen Z often balances financial caution with “treat yourself” spending.
  • Economic uncertainty changes how people think about long-term planning.
  • Avoiding money conversations may increase financial stress.
  • Financial habits reflect emotional needs, not just math.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Pexels

“Girl math” isn’t a new concept. It’s been all over social media for years now and has become so integrated into our culture that people use it as part of their vernacular when referring to excusable purchases. And while this is relatable and comedic, it’s really hiding the real conversation about how younger generations think about money.

At first glance, Gen Z’s financial habits can seem contradictory. They create detailed budgets, yet admit to impulse purchases. They worry about money but hesitate to ask a friend to pay them back for dinner. They want financial security while also embracing the idea of treating themselves after every “win” or slight inconvenience.

These behaviors, as inconsistent as they are, actually reflect something deeper: the psychology of growing up during prolonged economic uncertainty.

Every generation learns money differently

Financial habits are often shaped by family experiences, cultural expectations, and the economy in which people come of age.

For instance, many Baby Boomers entered adulthood during decades when homeownership felt attainable and stable employment often came with pensions or long-term career paths. Generation X experienced recessions but also witnessed rapid economic expansion. Similarly, Millennials graduated from college during the Great Recession and entered a scarce job market that redefined expectations around homeownership, debt, and career stability.

Gen Z inherited many of those same challenges while also navigating a global pandemic, record inflation, rising housing costs, and an increasingly unpredictable job market.

It’s difficult to plan confidently for a future that has often felt uncertain for them.

The rise of “soft-life budgeting”

A recent survey from Albert, a personal finance app, found that 64% of Gen Z would rather redo their entire monthly budget than ask a friend to pay them back for brunch. The survey also found that Gen Z is twice as likely to describe their spending as being based on “vibes,” while 57% admit that treating themselves is the category most likely to derail their budget.

When uncertainty becomes a constant part of life, people often begin balancing future planning with present-day emotional rewards. Small purchases like a coffee, a concert, or a quick weekend trip may become less about impulsivity and more about creating moments of predictability, enjoyment, and emotional regulation in an otherwise uncertain environment.

article continues after advertisement

A psychological concept known as uncertainty tolerance applies here. Uncertainty tolerance is our ability to cope with an unpredictable future. When people feel like major life goals are increasingly out of their control, whether it’s buying a home, paying off debt, or reaching financial stability, the brain naturally starts assigning more value to rewards that are available now.

When things seem too unattainable, our brain naturally looks for ways to gain control and create attainable moments of joy. The goal often isn’t the purchase itself, but the emotional experience attached to it.

That’s why these spending habits can seem contradictory. But it’s possible for someone to save money while also choosing experiences that improve their mood in the present. Rather than viewing these choices as irresponsible, it may be more helpful to understand them as an attempt to balance emotional well-being with long-term financial goals.

Is living for today really a bad thing?

Gen Z is often accused of focusing too much on instant gratification. But framing it that way overlooks the context in which many young adults came of age. When the future feels uncertain, prioritizing joy in the present isn’t always about impatience. It can also be a way of coping.

Research on uncertainty consistently shows that when people perceive the future as unpredictable, immediate rewards naturally become more valuable. If long-term goals, like buying a home, feel increasingly difficult to reach, smaller, attainable experiences can provide a sense of control and emotional well-being.

article continues after advertisement

That doesn’t necessarily mean Gen Z has abandoned future planning. It may mean they’re trying to find ways to enjoy life while planning for a future that feels less guaranteed than it did for previous generations.

More flexible budgeting and finding a balance

Traditionally, budgeting is seen as a restriction, allowing yourself to spend only a certain amount without any rewards.

Gen Z views budgeting as permission to spend in ways that align with personal values. Instead of asking, “What can't I spend money on? The question becomes, “What matters enough for me to spend money today?”

This means Gen Z may be saving up for a home, but it doesn’t mean they’re going to restrict their spending, even if only for a year or two. They'd rather take more time while also enjoying today.

Rather than judging this approach, it may be more helpful to understand the environment that shaped it. Gen Z entered adulthood during a period marked by economic instability, making flexibility feel more realistic than rigid financial rules.

Financial habits often reflect hope, fear, identity, and our beliefs about the future. Gen Z’s budgeting style isn’t necessarily evidence that they’re irresponsible or financially disengaged. If anything, it suggests they’re trying to navigate an economic reality that asks them to prepare for tomorrow while acknowledging that tomorrow isn’t always predictable.

Perhaps the healthiest approach isn’t choosing between saving and living, but learning how to do both.

item.title: A Better Version of Residential Dementia Care
item.description:
Dementia

A Better Version of Residential Dementia Care

Personal Perspective: The Hogeweyk charters a different course in dementia care.

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Residential advanced dementia care is often hard on the patients, their families, and their caregivers.
  • An institution in the Netherlands has revolutionized advanced dementia care.
  • The Hogeweyk creates as familiar a living environment as possible for dementia residents.
  • The Hogeweyk focuses on engagement in preserved interests and activities in its advanced dementia residents.

Imagine enabling people with severe dementia to live out their final months actively pursuing many of the interests and activities they had enjoyed throughout their lives, rather than being segregated from family and friends, sequestered into spartan hospital-like facilities, and medicated and sedated to near unconsciousness. Well, that is precisely the goal of the Hogeweyk, a residential dementia care facility located just a short train ride from the heart of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

Source: Pexels /Matosuky

Just a Typical Nursing Home

The center was formerly akin to most nursing homes—a one-size-fits-all experience for residents with long disorienting corridors of monotonous colorless resident rooms, overtaxed nurses, aides dispensing medications and meals on rigid schedules, residents spending much of their days deposited to unobtrusive corners of hallways and dayrooms, bored family members affecting shorter and shorter visits, limited interaction between residents, and an institutional focus on what residents could no longer accomplish for themselves.

But Then...

But then, a team of visionary professionals decided to flip the script. Residents were to be seen as and treated as individual independent beings—with their own personalities, values, past experiences, pursuits, pass-times, likes, and interests. Rather than treating residents as patients with a relentlessly progressive disease—losing function daily—the center focused on who each resident was throughout their lives and what they retained of their personas, their interests, and their activities, despite the disease. They were grouped by such retained qualities and encouraged to maintain them—even develop them further—independently and/or with others, with a focus on mobilization, movement, and activities of normal daily living. Care givers soon noted that despite often severe cognitive disabilities, most of the residents maintained some of the interests of their lives and pursued them joyfully when given the opportunity and support to do so.

Source: Pexels / İsra Nilgün Özkan

Life at the Hogeweyk

When an opportunity presented itself to rebuild the center, the Hogeweyk team did so to maximize their novel approach. The center is now arranged into twenty seven independent townhouse-style dwellings, each with a fully functional kitchen and spacious living room. Six or seven residents live in each house and are assisted by two attendants. Each resident has their own personalized bedroom and bathroom. There are four different types of housing interiors (from the conservative to the cosmopolitan) to coordinate with resident personalities and to facilitate a sense of familiarity. Within each house, residents are encouraged and supported to interact and to participate in activities of their choice. Many help with household chores such as cooking, cleaning, laundering etc.

article continues after advertisement

The houses enclose outdoor spaces where residents can walk about, breathe fresh air, take in the sun (and rain), interact, enjoy quiet gardens, and/or head for various facilities and club activities. These include a small fully functional supermarket where food and household necessities are purchased, a restaurant (where residents, families, and neighbors can gather and eat), a pub, a movie theatre/auditorium, a beauty parlor/barbershop, a fitness center, a music room, an arts and crafts room, and more. Clubs supporting various hobbies and interests are almost too numerous to count. One such club involves weekly gatherings in the pub for the singing of traditional Dutch folk songs.

To qualify for admission, residents need to be in end-stage dementia (with approximately 1-3 years of life expectancy) and need to have reached a point where they can no longer live independently or be cared for in the home of a family member. Despite this level of disability, on any given visit, one will witness residents milling about the various facilities with or without assistants, sitting out at picnic tables, partaking in club activities, visiting with their families, participating in therapy, laughing, interacting, cooking in their kitchens, doing crafts, reading papers, or watching TV in their living rooms. Few seem to be lying in their beds or sleeping in a wheelchair within view of a nurses station (of which there are none).

Source: Pexels / Kampus Production

Advantages of this System

Every year we take a group of Virginia Tech Neuroscience/Global Health Perspective students to visit the Hogeweyk. Most are intending to go into healthcare and many have worked within the American nursing home system. They are uniformly impressed and moved by the profound persistence of persona and personality, of activity and mobility, of physical robustness, of joy and verve, of interactive skills and drive, and of interest and motivation in the residents—in other words, of their preserved humanity. They note a stark difference between these residents and those in a traditional nursing facility. They also note the readily apparent presence of family members, children, and friends enjoying the plentiful and attractive communal spaces with the residents. They note that center feels like a little village rather than an institution. Yet, the administration at the Hogeweyk insists that the center receives no greater governmental funding than other Dutch dementia care facilities.

Acknowledgment and Acceptance of Death

One of the features that contributes to the center’s success is a realistic approach to end of life. The subject of death is not fastidiously avoided—by caregivers or family members. When it rears its head, death is not rabidly combated to the bitter end as if it was somehow a conquerable entity. Residents in terminal states are never subjected to weeks of ICU care, intubation, invasive procedures, and other tortures. Rather, the natural progression of the disease is acknowledged and accepted. With such an acknowledgement, however, impending death ceases to be a focus. Rather, optimized living is the focus. Readily reversible ailments are medically addressed as necessary, but devastating and/or preterminal events are addressed with expectant care centered on resident dignity and comfort.

article continues after advertisement

Caretakers maintain that with the Hogeweyk approach, residents are more robust, more physically capable, more alert, less confused, less depressed, less agitated than in a traditional center. They note that medication utilization for both behavioral and medical issues are significantly reduced. As a result, residents don’t seem to inexorably deteriorate month to month but, rather, maintain functionality until they are close to death, at which point they tend to rapidly deteriorate and peacefully succumb.

Source: Pexels / Kordanalev

Celebrating Meaningful Life

The ultimate focus of the center is a celebration of life until it comes to its natural end. There is far less a sense of warehousing of pre-terminal beings and far more a sense of indulging in the identities, activities, relationships that help define the best components of the human experience. The result is happier, more active and engaged residents, diminished stress and guilt in families (with greater involvement and engagement), and decreased stress and burnout in attendant caregivers. How this has not become the model for such care should be a question we are all asking.

item.title: Curly Fries With Cheese Can Be Healthier Than You Think
item.description:
Diet

Curly Fries With Cheese Can Be Healthier Than You Think

What's your motive when disparaging foods other people eat? Allergic to joy?

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional eating is not necessarily bad: If the emotions are positive, the experience can be a healthy one.
  • Unless you are asked to provide expert advice, judging the foods other people choose to eat is rude.
  • Shaming someone because you believe they could be a more attractive body shape doesn't make you a "caretaker."
  • If you hate what you eat, you won't necessarily live longer. It'll just seem longer because you're miserable.

Sitting next to someone who nags, “That’s over-processed” or “Do you really need that?” is worse for your health than eating curly fries with cheese.

As we are urged to monitor our intake of sodium and saturated fats when it comes to our own diets, we should probably also monitor our output of criticism and disparagement when it comes to the diets of others.

I’m not arguing that poutine should be classified as part of a heart-healthy diet; I am convinced that the French-Canadian signature dish (fries covered in rich brown gravy with cheese curds sprinkled throughout) can, with joy, be a more wholesome experience than eating amaranth and yogurt with a grudge and a spiteful attitude.

Research across the sciences has proven what instinct has always known: eating and emotions are inextricably linked. Many of these studies, understandably, focus on disordered eating.

If someone with severely disordered eating is close to you, they must get help. But if you disapprove of someone else’s pattern of eating because you judge them as being self-indulgent or overweight, do you feel a need to tell them how you feel? Are you sure you're helping them live better?

An in-depth 2023 article titled "The Association of Emotional Eating with Overweight/Obesity, Depression, Anxiety/Stress, and Dietary Patterns: A Review of the Current Clinical Evidence" published in "Nutrients" argues that "Eating caused by positive emotions was not related with negative outcomes," in all cases, according to data, and "Additionally, all types of emotional eating were not associated with worse self-reported physical health."

If you’ve never had ranch dressing, a Cornish beef pasty, or fried chicken on a waffle, do you want to shout—or worse, whisper loudly—"Do you have any idea how many calories you’re consuming?" because you feel a nearly overwhelming urge to point out the desperate danger of these items?

That urge doesn’t sound too healthy to me; you might want to get it examined.

I asked readers for their thoughts on being told what they should and should not eat. I asked specifically for their experiences concerning folks commenting on their meals when they weren’t asking for any advice.

Most responses indicated that being ritually nagged, shamed, or controlled during meals likely corrodes a person’s immune system, even as it undermines their sense of independence, self-esteem, and grasp on autonomy.

article continues after advertisement

“My ex-husband was a runner. He could eat anything and not gain weight,” explained Laura S. Nicholas-Schwab. “His constant badgering about food created a culture of cortisol for my nervous system. I lost weight following my divorce.”

Lisa D Saunders disentangled the food-bullying intervention from the context of weight gain or loss by declaring, simply, that “It’s the height of rudeness to comment on what someone is eating.” She goes on to give a delightful example: “Just last night I ordered a veggie burger with bacon. To my great pleasure, the server did not even raise an eyebrow. It was delicious.”

Susan Doust Young was put in the position of needing to defend her legal use of aspartame when “A nosy nerd berated our choice of Diet Coke at the checkout line, and I ignored him. What I should have said, however, was ‘I'm 78 years old. Mind your own damn business!’”

Eating is attached to emotion, and food is attached to territoriality. The implication of Kim Robinson’s response to my question about the implications of food-shaming was heartfelt: “It’s actually dangerous for their health” (don’t mess around with Kim), and her remark was echoed by Amy Hartl Sherman’s bark: “Anyone who questions my food choices out loud risks getting bit.”

If the shibboleth invoked to encourage the consumption of healthy foods is “You are what you eat,” there should be a caveat attached reminding us that few people choose to identify as rhubarb, kohlrabi, or yam.

Some of us still smile when called "Cookie" or "Sugar Pie," which we recall as words of endearment from our childhoods, as long as they're not said by a stranger, a boss, a warden, or worse, a politician. Somebody who calls me a "yam" better watch out, because I'm calling my friends Kim and Amy for backup.

Serve any dish you want, but leave out the big helpings of guilt, judgement, and nagging. Nobody wants those boxed up to bring home.
